1: Persian is written from right to left, but numbers are read left to right. There is no capital letter and no italic. The alphabet has 32 letters: the 28 Arabic letters plus four extra letters for Persian sounds (پ، چ، ژ، گ).

Letters join to the next letter inside a word, so each letter can have up to four shapes: isolated, initial, medial and final. Six letters never join to the letter after them: ا، د، ذ، ر، ز، ژ، و (seven if you count آ). After them the next letter starts a new shape, even inside the same word.
Persian added four letters to the Arabic alphabet. They look like a neighbouring letter with extra dots, so they are easy to remember.
father — پ = p (ب with three dots)
tea — چ = ch (ج with three dots)
jacket — ژ = zh as in 'measure' (ز with three dots)
cat — گ = g (ک with an extra stroke)
Many Arabic letters sound identical in Persian because they were borrowed with Arabic words. You must learn the spelling of each word, not only the sound.
⁣زیر zir · ذره zarre · ضرر zarar · ظرف zarf
Short vowels are usually not written

Persian has six vowels. The three long ones are written with letters (ا â, ی i, و u). The three short ones (a, e, o) are normally not written at all: کتاب is read ketâb, but only the letters k-t-b and the long vowel â are shown. In this app, the line under each word shows the pronunciation, so you can learn reading step by step.
2: Persian has three short vowels (a, e, o) and three long vowels (â, i, u). Length matters in careful speech, but the quality of the vowel also differs: â is a back, rounded vowel (close to the 'a' in 'water' for many speakers) and a is like the 'a' in 'cat'.

Two diphthongs exist: ey (as in 'say') and ow (as in 'go'). Persian also has two sounds that English lacks: kh (خ), like the 'ch' in Scottish 'loch', and gh (ق / غ), a voiced sound made at the back of the throat, like a French 'r'.

Stress falls on the last syllable of nouns and adjectives (ketÂB, dâneshJÚ), and on the first syllable of most verbs (MÍravam, NÁravam). Endings such as the plural -hâ and the ezafe -e do not take the stress.
3: Persian pronouns do not distinguish gender: او (u) means both 'he' and 'she'. The same pronoun is used as subject and object (the object marker را is added, see lesson 17). Subject pronouns are often dropped, because the verb ending already shows the person.

In speech, او is often replaced by اون (un), and آنها by اونا (unâ). The pronoun شما is used with strangers, older people, and in formal situations. Use تو only with close friends, family and children.
4: Persian has an independent verb (هستم، هستی، هست…) and a set of short endings (-am, -i, -ast…) that attach to the end of the previous word. Both mean 'am / are / is'. The independent forms are used for emphasis, for existence and in short answers; the endings are used inside sentences.
In writing, the endings attach with a small gap (a half-space) after words that end in a joining letter. Spoken Persian uses -e for است (خوب است → خوبه khube).
5: The normal word order is Subject + (time) + (place) + Object + Verb. The verb is always at the end of a simple sentence. Adjectives and possessors follow the noun.
To say 'I am not', use the verb نیستم and its forms. They replace both hastam and the endings.

A statement becomes a question just by changing the intonation (rising). In writing, you can add آیا (âyâ) at the start. Short answers: بله (bale, yes), آره (âre, yes – spoken), نه (na, no), خیر (kheyr, no – formal).
6: Persian has no word for 'the'. A bare noun can mean 'the book', 'a book' or 'books' depending on context. To stress 'one / a certain', put یک (yek) before the noun or add -ی (-i) to its end.
a good book (indefinite, the -i attaches to the whole phrase)
The common plural ending is ‌ها (-hâ) and it works for all nouns. The ending ‌ان (-ân) is used for people and for some living things or in written style. After a number, the noun stays singular.
7: Question words stay in the position of the answer, usually just before the verb. Intonation is falling, not rising.
8: To say 'my book', 'your book' and so on, Persian attaches a short ending to the noun. There is no separate word for 'my'.

After a word that ends in ا or و, a linking ی is added before the ending: پا → پایم (pâyam, my foot). After silent -ه (as in خانه) the ending attaches directly with a half-space: خانه‌ام (khâneam, my house). The long form کتابِ من (ketâb-e man) means the same and is used when you want to stress 'mine'.
9: The ezafe is a short vowel -e (ِ) that links a noun to the word that describes it (adjective, possessor or another noun). It is almost never written, but always pronounced. The head noun comes first: 'book-e good' = good book.
After the vowels ا and و the ezafe is pronounced -ye and written ی. After silent -ه it is -ye too (written ‌ی or the sign ٔ). Ezafes can be chained: each noun links to the next.
the big university of the city
10: Adjectives never change for gender or number. They stand after the noun and are joined to it by the ezafe: خانهٔ بزرگ (a big house), خانه‌های بزرگ (big houses). After 'to be' they stand alone: خانه بزرگ است.
Add -تر (-tar) for 'more' and -ترین (-tarin) for 'most'. 'Than' is از (az). The irregular forms are بهتر (behtar, better) and بهترین (behtarin, best).
⁣این خانه از آن خانه بزرگ‌تر است.
⁣in khâne az ân khâne bozorg-tar ast.
This house is bigger than that house.
11: Persian uses its own digits: ۰ ۱ ۲ ۳ ۴ ۵ ۶ ۷ ۸ ۹. Note that ۴ ۵ ۶ look different from the Arabic digits and that 0 is a dot. Numbers are written left to right.
After a number the noun stays singular. For people, the counter نفر (nafar) is common; for things you can add عدد (adad). The counter is optional in speech.
12: Compound numbers join with و (-o): ۲۱ = بیست و یک (bist-o yek). Hundreds are written as one word: ۲۰۰ = دویست (divist).
Ordinals are formed with -م (-om): پنج → پنجم (panjom, fifth). Irregular: اول (avval, first), دوم (dovvom, second), سوم (sevvom, third). In formal style you may also use -مین (-omin).
13: Present tense = می‌ (mi-) + present stem + personal ending. The prefix می‌ is written separately with a half-space. It expresses both habit ('I drink tea') and action in progress ('I am drinking tea').
Present of the verb 'to eat' (stem: خور khor)

The subject pronoun is usually left out, because the ending shows who is acting. The infinitive always ends in -دن or -تن (-dan / -tan); the present stem often differs from the infinitive, so it has to be memorised (see the next lesson).
14: Each verb has two stems: the past stem (the infinitive minus -ن) and the present stem. Many present stems are irregular. Learn them together with the infinitive.
15: In the present tense the negative prefix نمی‌ (nemi-) replaces می‌. In other tenses the prefix ن- (na-) is added in front of the verb. The stress moves to the negative prefix.
Persian allows only one negation: words like هیچ (hich, no) and هرگز (hargez, never) go with a verb that is itself negative.
16: Prepositions come before the noun. Longer prepositions (روی، زیر، کنار، جلوی…) are linked to the noun with the ezafe.
The book is on the table.
He / she goes with his / her friend.
17: را (râ) marks a definite or specific direct object. It stands directly after the object (not after the verb). If the object is indefinite and general, را is not used.
In everyday speech را is shortened to -ro (after a consonant) or -ro / -o (after a vowel) and joined to the word: کتابو (ketâbo), او رو (u ro).
18: The Iranian week starts on Saturday and the weekend is Friday (Thursday is often a half-holiday).
Iran uses the solar Hijri calendar. The year starts on Nowruz (about 21 March). The first six months have 31 days, the next five 30 days, and Esfand 29 or 30.
19: این (in) means 'this' and آن (ân) means 'that'. Their plurals are اینها (inhâ) and آنها (ânhâ). They stand before the noun and do not change. In speech, آن becomes اون (un).
To say that something exists ('there is'), use هست (hast) or the verb وجود دارد (vojud dârad). Negative: نیست (nist). The place usually stands at the beginning of the sentence.
There is a table in the room.
There are two books on the table.
20: The imperative is formed with the prefix ب- (be-) plus the present stem. For تو there is no ending; for شما add -ید. The negative prefix is ن- (na-).
With compound verbs the prefix be- is omitted: کمک کن (komak kon, help!). To be polite add لطفاً (lotfan), or ask with «ممکن است … ؟» (momken ast…, is it possible…?).
21: After خواستن (khâstan, want) and توانستن (tavânestan, can) the second verb is in the subjunctive: ب- + present stem + ending (بروم، بروی، برود، برویم، بروید، بروند). Both verbs take the same person.
We do not want to go.
باید (bâyad, must / have to) and نباید (nabâyad, must not) are invariable; the verb after them is in the subjunctive and shows the person.
22: Most Persian verbs are compounds: a noun or adjective plus a light verb such as کردن (kardan, do), شدن (shodan, become), زدن (zadan, hit), دادن (dâdan, give), داشتن (dâshtan, have), گرفتن (gereftan, take). Only the light verb is conjugated.
23: Persian has a formal written style and an informal spoken style. Newspapers, books and official speech use the written form; conversation and films use the spoken one. Most pronunciation changes are regular, so you can learn them as rules.

Learn to read written Persian first, but listen to spoken Persian from the start. The app lets you hear both: words are shown in the formal form, and examples show the more common spoken forms in brackets where useful.
24: Persian has an informal 'you' (تو) and a polite 'you' (شما). Use شما with anyone you do not know well, with older people and in formal situations. Respectful speech may also use the third-person plural for one person: ایشان تشریف آوردند (ishân tashrif âvardand, he / she has kindly come).
(lit. may you not be tired) said to someone working

Taarof is the Persian system of ritual politeness: you may refuse an offer several times before accepting, and the host insists several times. A price of «قابلی ندارد» (ghâboli nadârad, 'it is not worthy of you') does not mean the thing is free. Learn it as culture: when in doubt, thank, refuse once politely, and accept when the offer is repeated.
25: Persian distinguishes paternal and maternal relatives: your father's brother is عمو (amu) and your mother's brother is دایی (dâyi); your father's sister is عمه (ameh) and your mother's sister is خاله (khâle).
⁣من دو برادر و یک خواهر دارم.
⁣man do barâdar o yek khâhar dâram.
I have two brothers and one sister.
26: Combine what you have learned: S – time – place – object (+ را) – verb. Add a question word before the verb, a negative prefix on the verb, and the ezafe between noun and adjective.
⁣من هر روز در دانشگاه فارسی می‌خوانم.
⁣man har ruz dar dâneshgâh fârsi mikhânam.
I study Persian at the university every day.
I do not want that book.
I am fine, thank you. And you?
I am fine too. What is your name?
⁣اسم من علی است. از آشنایی شما خوشحالم.
⁣esm-e man Ali ast. az âshnâyi-ye shomâ khoshhâlam.
My name is Ali. Pleased to meet you.
27: The past stem is the infinitive without the final -ن (raftan → raft, khordan → khord). The endings are -am, -i, (nothing), -im, -id, -and. The 3rd person singular has no ending, and the stress falls on the last syllable of the stem.
The simple past tells what happened and is finished. The negative prefix is نـ (na-), and it takes the stress: نرفتم (NAraftam).
Yesterday I went to the university.
We did not see the film.
28: Most past stems are simply the infinitive without -ن. The present stem is often different. Learn both together; the table shows the 3rd person singular past and the I-form present.
Many verbs show the pattern -یدن / -یدن (khâbidan, to sleep → khâbid) and -استن (khâstan → khâst, to want). Learn the 5–10 most frequent irregular verbs by heart; the rest are regular.
29: To describe a repeated or habitual past action, or an action that was in progress, use می‌ + past stem + endings. English translates it as 'used to…' or 'was …ing'.
I used to go to the park every day.
When I was a child, I used to drink milk.
He / she was reading a book.

To stress that an action is happening right now, use داشتن (dâshtan) before the main verb, in the matching tense: دارم می‌روم (dâram miravam, I am going), داشتم می‌رفتم (dâshtam miraftam, I was going).
30: The past participle is the past stem + ه (raftan → rafte). The enclitic forms of 'to be' follow it: رفته‌ام (rafte-am), رفته‌ای, رفته است, رفته‌ایم, رفته‌اید, رفته‌اند. It is used for past events with a connection to now, or with experience.
Have you ever been to Iran?
I have never eaten this food.
31: The formal future is formed with the present of خواستن (khâstan) and the past stem of the main verb: خواهم رفت (khâham raft, I will go). The auxiliary comes before the verb, and the personal ending goes on the auxiliary. In the negative, ن- attaches to the auxiliary.
In speech the future is simply the present tense with a time expression: فردا می‌روم (fardâ miravam). The formal future appears in news and writing.
I am going to Tehran tomorrow.
I will see you next week.
32: Subjunctive = ب- (be-) + present stem + endings. Compound verbs and some verbs omit the prefix. The verb 'to be' has its own subjunctive: باشم، باشی، باشد، باشیم، باشید، باشند.

The subjunctive follows modal verbs and expressions of wish, necessity, doubt and purpose: می‌خواهم (I want), باید (must), شاید (perhaps), تا (so that), قبل از اینکه (before), بعد از اینکه… (after, with either mood).
Perhaps he / she will come tomorrow.
In order to understand, I read it again.
You must go to sleep early.
33: Modal expressions are followed by a subjunctive verb. باید is invariable; می‌توانم and می‌خواهم are conjugated; ممکن است (momken ast, it is possible) is used for permission and politeness.
Would you like something to drink?
It would be better to leave early.
You do not need to come.
34: A realistic condition uses اگر (agar) + subjunctive or present; the main clause is in the present, future or imperative.
If it rains, I will stay at home.
⁣اگر وقت داشته باشی، به من زنگ بزن.
⁣agar vaght dâshte bâshi, be man zang bezan.
If you have time, call me.
If you want, I will help.
Besides اگر, use: در صورتی که (dar surati ke, in case that), مگر اینکه (magar inke, unless). The spoken form is اگه (age).
I will come unless it rains.
35: I want tea but not coffee.
I came late because there was traffic.
Therefore I have to leave earlier.
36: To compare two things, use adjective + -تر + از. To say that two things are equal use به اندازهٔ (be andâze-ye) or مثل (mesl-e). 'The most' is -ترین before or after the noun. 'Too' is بیش از حد (bish az had) or خیلی.
He / she is taller than me.
⁣این کتاب به اندازهٔ آن کتاب خوب است.
⁣in ketâb be andâze-ye ân ketâb khub ast.
This book is as good as that one.
He / she is like his / her father.
37: Frequency adverbs stand before the verb (or at the start of the sentence). They do not change form.
38: The word که (ke, 'that / who / which') introduces relative clauses and noun clauses. The head noun usually takes an indefinite -ی (-i) before که.
The book that I bought was good.
⁣مردی که آنجا ایستاده است، معلم من است.
⁣mardi ke ânjâ istâde ast, mo'allem-e man ast.
The man who is standing there is my teacher.
I know that he / she has come.

In Persian the relative pronoun is not repeated by an extra pronoun when it refers to the subject. When it is the object, the object marker را is left out of the relative clause, but kept if the noun with که is itself the object of the main verb.
The girl you saw is my sister.
I liked the book that I read.
39: ‌ها is the default plural. ‌ان is common for people and some animals, and in poetry or written style for other nouns. Arabic loanwords may keep an Arabic plural (-ât, -in, broken plurals), which you should learn as vocabulary.
A plural subject normally takes a plural verb, but when the subject is non-human it often takes a singular verb: «کتاب‌ها روی میز است» is natural. Nouns with numbers stay singular.
The children are playing in the yard.
The trees are big. (non-human plural, singular verb)
40: خود (khod) means 'self'. With a possessive ending it forms a reflexive pronoun. It is used for emphasis ('I myself') and as the object of reflexive verbs.
I saw myself in the mirror.
41: The passive is formed with the past participle and the verb شدن (shodan). The agent can be added with توسط or به وسیلهٔ (tavassot-e, be vasile-ye).
This book was written by him / her.
Persian often avoids the passive by using the 3rd person plural of an active verb: می‌گویند (they say = it is said), ساختند (they built).
They say it will rain tomorrow.
42: Quantifiers come before the noun, which usually stays singular after a number or quantity word.
Some of my friends are Iranian.
43: Excuse me, where is the metro station?
After the bank, it's on the left.
44: دوست داشتن (dust dâshtan) is used for 'to like' and 'to love'. علاقه داشتن به (alâghe dâshtan be) means 'to be interested in'. ترجیح دادن (tarjih dâdan) means 'to prefer'.
I prefer to stay at home.
45: To say that something hurts, use the body part with a possessive ending + درد می‌کند (dard mikonad): سرم درد می‌کند (my head hurts). With nouns you can say «… درد دارم» (… dard dâram).
This is language for visiting a doctor; it is not medical advice. If you feel unwell, call the local emergency number.
I need pills and a prescription.
46: Iranians say prices in tomans in speech, but the official currency is the rial (1 toman = 10 rials). Large prices are said with هزار (thousand) and میلیون (million).
Don't you have a cheaper one?
47: Excuse me, is Mr. Rezaei there?
Could you give me your number?
A formal letter starts with با سلام و احترام (bâ salâm o ehterâm) and ends with با تشکر (bâ tashakkor) or با احترام (bâ ehterâm). 'Attachment' is پیوست (peyvast), 'subject' is موضوع (mowzu').
Dear Sir / Madam (lit. with greetings and respect)
49: What does he / she look like?
He / she has black hair and brown eyes.
50: I want a ticket to Shiraz.
What time does the train leave?
Where does the bus to the university stop?
52: Because it is cold, I wear a coat.
53: Refusing once and then accepting is part of taarof. If you really do not want something, refuse firmly but politely: «ممنون، میل ندارم» (mamnun, meyl nadâram).
Thank you, I don't want any.
That is very kind of you.
58: When you tell a story use the simple past for the main events and the past continuous for background or repeated actions.
⁣دیروز صبح زود از خواب بیدار شدم.
⁣diruz sobh zud az khâb bidâr shodam.
Yesterday morning I woke up early.
I took a shower and had breakfast.
When I was going to the university it was raining.
59: I want to open an account.
62: What do you do on weekends?
67: I want to become a doctor.
Next year I'm going to Iran.
68: A2 review: telling a short story
Yesterday I went to the park with my friend.
⁣هوا آفتابی بود و بچه‌ها بازی می‌کردند.
⁣havâ âftâbi bud o bachche-hâ bâzi mikardand.
The weather was sunny and children were playing.
⁣بعد از آن چای نوشیدیم و به خانه برگشتیم.
⁣ba'd az ân châi nushidim o be khâne bargashtim.
After that we drank tea and went back home.
70: The past perfect (pluperfect) uses the past participle with the past of 'to be' (بود): رفته بودم (rafte budam, I had gone). It shows that an action happened before another past action.
When I arrived, he / she had left.
I had read this book before.
The negative prefix goes on the participle: نرفته بودم (narafte budam, I had not gone).
⁣تا آن موقع او را ندیده بودم.
⁣tâ ân moghe' u râ nadide budam.
Until then I had not seen him / her.
74: The past subjunctive = past participle + the subjunctive of 'to be' (باشم، باشی، باشد…): رفته باشم (rafte bâsham). It expresses doubt, hope or probability about a completed action.
I hope you have finished the work.
Use with conditions and time clauses
After اگر and بعد از اینکه the past subjunctive can express 'if … has happened'.
⁣اگر نامه را فرستاده باشی، لازم نیست دوباره بفرستی.
⁣agar nâme râ ferestâde bâshi, lâzem nist dobâre befresti.
If you have sent the letter, you don't need to send it again.
78: For an unreal present or future, use the past continuous in both clauses: اگر پول داشتم، سفر می‌کردم. For an unreal past, use the past perfect (or past continuous) in both clauses: اگر رفته بودم، او را دیده بودم.
If I had money, I would travel.
⁣اگر زودتر آمده بودی، او را می‌دیدی.
⁣agar zudtar âmade budi, u râ mididi.
If you had come earlier, you would have seen him / her.
If I were you, I would go.
کاش (kâsh, 'if only') is followed by the past continuous (present wish) or past perfect (past wish).
I wish I had come earlier.
82: Many intransitive verbs form a causative by adding -اندن to the present stem: رسیدن (to arrive) → رساندن (to deliver, to make arrive). The subject makes someone / something do the action.
to jump / fly → to make fly
Many causatives are made with compound verbs: خراب شدن → خراب کردن (to break down → to ruin), تمام شدن → تمام کردن (to end → to finish).
86: Indirect speech uses که (ke, 'that'). Persian does not shift tenses as English does: the verb stays in the tense of the original speech. Pronouns are adjusted.
Ali said that he is coming (would come).
He / she asked where you are going.
I told him / her to come.
He / she asked me to help.
I don't know where he / she is.
90: In informal speech verb endings shorten in regular ways. You need these to understand films, songs and everyday conversation.
95: Persian forms many nouns by adding a suffix to the present stem: -ش (-esh), -ار (-âr), -نده (-ande, agent), -ی (-i, abstract), -گی (-gi, quality).
The infinitive can be used as a noun: خواندن (reading), نوشتن (writing). It stands as subject or object.
100: Persian forms many verbs from a simple verb and a prefix like بر- (bar-), در- (dar-), باز- (bâz-), فرو- (foru-), وا- (vâ-). The meaning is often idiomatic, so learn them as a unit.
⁣ketâb râ az ru-ye miz bar dâshtam.
I picked the book up from the table.
I come back from my trip tomorrow.
105: The present participle is the present stem + -ان (-ân) or -نده (-ande): خندان (smiling), روشن‌کننده. The past participle ends in -ه (-e) and works as an adjective: شکسته (broken), بسته (closed).
110: Clauses of time are introduced by وقتی که، هر وقت، همین که، تا وقتی که، بعد از اینکه، قبل از اینکه. 'Before' takes the subjunctive; 'after' usually takes the past or present perfect.
As soon as I saw him / her, I laughed.
⁣قبل از اینکه بروم، به شما زنگ می‌زنم.
⁣ghabl az inke beravam, be shomâ zang mizanam.
Before I leave, I'll call you.
115: Concession is expressed with با اینکه، اگرچه، هرچند، با وجود اینکه (although) followed by an indicative verb, and ولی، اما، با این حال (but, nevertheless) between clauses.
Although I was tired, I worked.
Even though it's expensive, I'll buy it.
120: Purpose is expressed with تا (tâ) or برای اینکه (barâ-ye inke) + subjunctive. Result uses به طوری که (be towri ke) + indicative.
I study so that I succeed.
I'll say it again so that you understand.
He / she was so tired that he / she fell asleep.
130: Ezafe chains can include several nouns and adjectives. The ezafe is not used between a noun and a following demonstrative or number, or after a vocative, and not before a verb. The word order with relative clauses: noun + (-i) + که.
the new book of the university professor
Many nouns used as prepositions take ezafe: بعد از، پیش از، در مورد، در برابر، به‌خاطر.
140: A large part of formal Persian vocabulary comes from Arabic, built on three-letter roots and fixed patterns. Recognising patterns helps you guess meanings.
Some Arabic words keep Arabic plural forms: -ات (-ât), -ین (-in) for people and broken plurals. In modern Persian the plural -ها is also widely used.
150: In formal speech, Persian uses special respectful verbs and the pronoun ایشان for third persons.
Speakers lower themselves: «خدمت شما عرض می‌کنم» (khedmat-e shomâ arz mikonam, I submit to you), and «بنده» (bande, your servant) for 'I'.
It is not worthy of you (said when giving a gift).
160: A formal e-mail has: salutation (جناب آقای / سرکار خانم + name), opening (با سلام و احترام), the body, a closing (با تشکر و احترام) and your name.
Dear Sir / Madam (with greetings and respect)
172: B1 review: reading a short news item
News Persian uses formal verbs, passive and impersonal forms, and sentences with several که-clauses. Read for the main verb at the end, then go back to the subject.
⁣رئیس‌جمهور در سخنرانی خود اعلام کرد که پروژه تا پایان سال تمام خواهد شد.
⁣ra'is-jomhur dar sokhanrâni-ye khod e'lâm kard ke proje tâ pâyân-e sâl tamâm khâhad shod.
The president announced in his speech that the project would be finished by the end of the year.
⁣بر اساس گزارش‌ها، این طرح اجرا شده است.
⁣bar asâs-e gozâresh-hâ, in tarh ejrâ shode ast.
According to the reports, the plan has been carried out.
180: Complex Persian sentences place subordinate که-clauses before the final verb. The main verb stays at the end; modifiers come before the noun phrase via ezafe or the relative که.
⁣می‌دانم که او گفته است که فردا خواهد آمد.
⁣midânam ke u gofte ast ke fardâ khâhad âmad.
I know that he / she has said that he / she will come tomorrow.

The one who did this must answer for it.
190: Use شاید + subjunctive, احتمالاً (probably), ظاهراً (apparently), به نظر می‌رسد که (it seems that), and باید + past subjunctive for logical deduction.
It seems that it is raining.
200: Academic and official Persian uses impersonal constructions: گفته می‌شود، دیده می‌شود، باید توجه کرد، لازم به ذکر است (it should be mentioned).
210: News texts use a set of reporting verbs: اعلام کرد (announced), اظهار داشت (stated), افزود (added), تأکید کرد (emphasised), گفت (said). The pronoun وی (vey) means 'he / she' in formal writing.
220: Idioms are central to fluent Persian. Learn them as whole units.
to waste effort (lit. to pound water in a mortar)
the true motive shows (lit. the rooster's tail)
⁣دو صد گفته چون نیم کردار نیست.
⁣do sad gofte chon nim kerdâr nist.
Two hundred words are not worth half a deed.
235: Good written Persian relies on connectors to structure arguments.
on the one hand … on the other …
247: A typical essay: introduction (مقدمه) with a thesis; body (بدنه) with arguments and examples; conclusion (نتیجه‌گیری). Use connectors, rhetorical questions and the passive for objectivity.
255: Persian has three broad styles: colloquial (گفتاری), standard written (نوشتاری) and literary / classical (ادبی). They differ in vocabulary, verb forms and word order; literary style may place the verb earlier, use older forms (همی، بدین) and omit the subject.
262: Classical Persian poetry is built from couplets (بیت, beyt) of two half-lines (مصراع, mesrâ'). A ghazal has 5–15 couplets; the second half-lines of all couplets share a rhyme (قافیه, ghâfiye) and often a refrain (ردیف, radif). Poets include Ferdowsi (Shahnameh), Sa'di, Hafez, Rumi (Mowlavi) and Khayyam (quatrains, رباعی).
Poetry follows quantitative meters (عروض): short and long syllables. Short vowels are pronounced as the meter requires, and the ezafe may be lengthened. Reading aloud helps.
269: Aspect in Persian: می- marks the imperfective; bare past stems mark perfective events. Modality: باید + past subjunctive for deduction, می‌بایست (mibâyest) for obligation in the past, می‌توانست (mitavânest) for possibility in the past.
He / she must be at home (deduction).
He / she was supposed to come.
272: Traditional Persian rhetoric (بلاغت) distinguishes: تشبیه (tashbih, simile), استعاره (este'âre, metaphor), کنایه (kenâye, indirect expression), ایهام (ihâm, double meaning), اغراق (eghrâgh, exaggeration), تلمیح (talmih, allusion).
indirect expression (e.g. 'to have a long hand' = to be powerful)
274: To read real texts: first find the verb (end of the sentence), then the subject, then follow the ezafe chains left to right (noun-e adjective-e noun). Recognise Arabic patterns, and use the context for the many compound verbs. Keep a personal list of idioms and connectors; and read both news and short stories regularly.
